---
title: "Refinements to Rceattle for eastern Bering Sea pollock"

bibliography: references.bib

abstract: |
  The custom AD Model Builder (ADMB) stock assessment model developed for eastern Bering Sea
  walleye pollock has a long history of application. For a variety of
  reasons, including general recommendations from the 2025 Center for
  Independent Experts (CIE) reviews, the custom ADMB code has been
  successfully ported to R Template Model Builder (RTMB). That
  conversion provides access to advanced RTMB features and makes the
  underlying code easier to understand and modify. Similarly, adopting
  more generic platforms, such as Rceattle, can provide access to more
  modern software developments. In this study, we tailored Rceattle code
  and configurations so that Rceattle can closely mimic the custom
  ADMB/RTMB assessment code. The Rceattle configuration uses the supported
  AFSC multinomial composition likelihood and a non-parametric
  selectivity form. We also evaluated a
  two-dimensional, first-order autoregressive (AR1) selectivity sensitivity;
  it did not converge and remains a research topic. An exploratory dynamic
  structural equation modeling (DSEM) analysis shows how recruitment
  covariates can be compared by cohort, separately from the final assessment
  configuration.

```{r}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) {
  if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) y else x
}

project_file <- function(...) {
  normalizePath(file.path(project_root, ...), mustWork = FALSE)
}

parse_asar_glossary <- function(path) {
  glossary_lines <- trimws(readLines(path, warn = FALSE))
  pattern <- "^\\\\newacronym\\{([^}]*)\\}\\{([^}]*)\\}\\{([^}]*)\\}$"
  matches <- regmatches(glossary_lines, regexec(pattern, glossary_lines))
  matches <- matches[lengths(matches) == 4]
  tibble(
    label = vapply(matches, `[[`, character(1), 2),
    Acronym = vapply(matches, `[[`, character(1), 3),
    Definition = vapply(matches, `[[`, character(1), 4)
  )
}

project_glossary <- parse_asar_glossary(project_file("report_glossary.tex"))

absolute_or_project <- function(path) {
  if (grepl("^file://", path)) {
    return(normalizePath(sub("^file://", "", path), mustWork = FALSE))
  }
  if (grepl("^/", path)) {
    normalizePath(path, mustWork = FALSE)
  } else {
    project_file(path)
  }
}

file_size <- function(path) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    return(NA_character_)
  }
  paste0(formatC(file.info(path)$size / 1024, format = "f", digits = 1), " KB")
}

read_admb_vector <- function(path, key) {
  lines <- readLines(path)
  start <- grep(paste0("^", key, "$"), lines)[1]
  if (is.na(start)) {
    return(tibble(Year = integer(), Value = numeric()))
  }

  rows <- list()
  i <- start + 1
  while (i <= length(lines)) {
    values <- suppressWarnings(
      as.numeric(strsplit(trimws(lines[i]), " +")[[1]])
    )
    if (anyNA(values) || length(values) < 2) {
      break
    }
    rows[[length(rows) + 1]] <- values[1:2]
    i <- i + 1
  }

  as_tibble(do.call(rbind, rows), .name_repair = "minimal") |>
    setNames(c("Year", "Value"))
}

check_messages <- function(fit, levels = c("WARN", "FAIL")) {
  checks <- fit$convergence$checks %||% list()
  messages <- vapply(checks, function(check) {
    severity <- check$severity %||% NA_character_
    if (is.na(severity) || !severity %in% levels) {
      return(NA_character_)
    }
    check$message %||% NA_character_
  }, character(1))

  messages <- messages[!is.na(messages)]
  if (length(messages) == 0) {
    "None"
  } else {
    paste(messages, collapse = "; ") |>
      gsub(
        pattern = "Hessian not invertible",
        replacement = "Hessian inversion failed",
        fixed = TRUE
      )
  }
}

objective_value <- function(fit) {
  value <- fit$opt$objective %||% fit$opt$opt$objective %||% NA_real_
  as.numeric(value)
}

convergence_row <- function(label, fit) {
  max_gradient <- fit$convergence$checks$max_gradient$data$max_gradient %||%
    NA_real_
  worst_param <- fit$convergence$checks$max_gradient$data$worst$param %||%
    NA_character_
  pd_hessian <- fit$convergence$checks$max_gradient$data$pdHess %||% NA

  tibble(
    Model = label,
    Status = fit$convergence$status %||% NA_character_,
    Objective = objective_value(fit),
    Max_gradient = max_gradient,
    Worst_parameter = worst_param,
    Positive_definite_Hessian = as.character(pd_hessian),
    Warnings_or_failures = check_messages(fit)
  )
}

comparison_summary <- quantity_long |>
  filter(!is.na(Method)) |>
  select(Year, Quantity, Method, Value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = Method, values_from = Value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("Rceattle"),
    names_to = "Method",
    values_to = "Estimate"
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(Estimate), is.finite(`ADMB reference`), `ADMB reference` > 0) |>
  group_by(Method, Quantity) |>
  arrange(Year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  summarise(
    Correlation = cor(Estimate, `ADMB reference`),
    Mean_absolute_percent = mean(abs(100 * (Estimate / `ADMB reference` - 1))),
    Max_absolute_percent = max(abs(100 * (Estimate / `ADMB reference` - 1))),
    Terminal_percent = dplyr::last(100 * (Estimate / `ADMB reference` - 1)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Method = recode(
      Method,
      `Rceattle NonParametricPM` = "Rceattle configuration",
      `Rceattle standard multinomial` = "Standard multinomial sensitivity",
      `Rceattle 2D AR1` = "Historical 2D AR1 sensitivity"

  filter(is.finite(Selectivity), Age >= 1, Age <= 15) |>
  group_by(Model, Year) |>
  mutate(Relative_selectivity = Selectivity / max(Selectivity, na.rm = TRUE)) |>

    Data_group,
    n,
    sdnr,
    sdnr_lo,
    sdnr_hi,
    lower,
    upper,
    Pass

make_afscosa_composition <- function(fleet_code) {
  fit <- fits$nonparametric_pm
  comp_data <- fit$data_list$comp_data
  rows <- which(comp_data$Fleet_code == fleet_code)

  # afscOSA converts proportions to integer counts. A row is informative
  # only when that conversion retains at least one observation.
  valid <- rowSums(
    round(
      comp_data$Sample_size[rows] *
        fit$quantities$comp_obs[rows, , drop = FALSE]
    )
  ) >= 1
  rows <- rows[valid]
  years <- comp_data$Year[rows]

  internal_osa <- osa |>
    filter(
      source == "comp",
      fleet == fleet_code,
      year %in% years
    ) |>
    arrange(match(year, years), age_length_bin)

  n_bins <- ncol(fit$quantities$comp_obs)
  stopifnot(nrow(internal_osa) == length(rows) * (n_bins - 1L))
  osa_matrix <- matrix(
    internal_osa$residual,
    nrow = length(rows),
    ncol = n_bins - 1L,
    byrow = TRUE
  )

  afscOSA::run_osa(
    obs = fit$quantities$comp_obs[rows, , drop = FALSE],
    exp = fit$quantities$comp_hat[rows, , drop = FALSE],
    N = comp_data$Sample_size[rows],
    fleet = comp_data$Fleet_name[rows[1]],
    index = seq_len(n_bins),
    years = years,
    index_label = "Age",
    res = osa_matrix
  )
}

afscosa_composition <- lapply(c(1, 3, 4), make_afscosa_composition)

convergence_summary <- bind_rows(
  convergence_row("Stage 1 scale fit", fits$stage_a),
  convergence_row("Rceattle fit", fits$nonparametric_pm),
  convergence_row("Standard multinomial sensitivity", fits$standard_multinomial),
  convergence_row("2D AR1 selectivity sensitivity", fits$ar1_2d)
)
```

## Executive Summary

Building from the ADMB-to-RTMB conversion, this analysis evaluates
whether Rceattle can be configured to reproduce the main features of
the 2024 eastern Bering Sea pollock "PM" assessment while providing a
model that is easier to extend. This 5.8.1 update focuses on
the Rceattle configuration, comparison with the modified ADMB model,
model diagnostics, and projection inputs.

When the Rceattle parameters and fishery selectivity are set to the same values
used in the ADMB model, Rceattle reproduces numbers-at-age, spawning biomass,
and predicted catch to numerical precision. Mean absolute differences are
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "SSB mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for spawning biomass and
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Catch mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for predicted catch. This result establishes agreement in the population
dynamics when both implementations use the same parameter values.

When Rceattle was fit to the data, it reached `OK` convergence status with a
positive-definite Hessian. The least-identified direction remained in annual
ATS/AVO selectivity deviations, but the added direct coefficient-increment
penalty reduced the condition number below the warning threshold. Relative to the
ADMB fit, mean absolute differences were
`r sprintf("%.1f", comparison_summary$Mean_absolute_percent[comparison_summary$Method == "Rceattle configuration" & comparison_summary$Quantity == "Spawning biomass"])`%
for spawning biomass,
`r sprintf("%.1f", comparison_summary$Mean_absolute_percent[comparison_summary$Method == "Rceattle configuration" & comparison_summary$Quantity == "Recruitment"])`%
for recruitment, and
`r sprintf("%.1f", comparison_summary$Mean_absolute_percent[comparison_summary$Method == "Rceattle configuration" & comparison_summary$Quantity == "Total biomass"])`%
for total biomass. These small differences are concentrated in the earliest
years; the remaining uncertainty is primarily estimability of the annual
selectivity deviations.

The 2D age-by-year AR1 selectivity sensitivity was included as an
initial diagnostic attempt. Results appeared broadly similar to the
non-parametric constrained selectivity fits. However, because some
parameters reached bounds, the model failed to converge. Closer
examination of this selectivity form will continue as a research topic.

One-step-ahead residuals and nine terminal-year-consistent retrospective
peels have been generated from the Rceattle configuration. Aggregate
composition residual dispersion is lower than the standard-normal reference. Mohn's rho
is
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Spawning biomass"])`
for spawning biomass,
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Total biomass"])`
for total biomass,
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Recruitment"])`
for recruitment, and
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Fishing mortality"])`
for fishing mortality. Forty-eight of 50 jitters returned to the best solution;
two found a substantially poorer mode. These results focus subsequent work on
selectivity identification, retrospective bias, and observation-model
sensitivity.

## Purpose and Scope

The September 2026 review focuses on whether the Rceattle configuration
has sufficient documentation for Plan Team evaluation. This working
paper serves that focused purpose rather than the broader purpose of a
full Stock Assessment and Fishery Evaluation (SAFE) chapter.

This working paper therefore records:

- what was run from those development files;
- how the Rceattle outputs compare with the modified ADMB reference;
- which diagnostics are available now;
- which sensitivities remain research-only; and
- what work would help structure the next evaluation pass.

The report uses the [Alaska Stock Assessment Report (`asar`)
package](https://github.com/nmfs-ost/asar) for glossary conventions and
accessibility guidance [@schiano2026asar]. Those practices helped prepare the
Quarto source for Section 508 review, including semantic headings and tables,
descriptive figure captions, and alternative text. They support accessibility
but do not replace final manual and agency-approved compliance checks.

Standard SAFE report sections such as background material, fishery
history, ecosystem narrative, reference-point tables, and harvest advice
are outside the scope of this document. Projection calculations are
included only to test the export and use of the Rceattle results.

## Rceattle Configuration

### Model Inputs

The Rceattle configuration uses the prepared workbook
`Data/EBS_24_pollock_m23_rceattle_full_1964-2024.xlsx`. The data builder retains
every age from 1 through 15. Fishery compositions use nominal sample sizes;
bottom trawl survey (BTS) and acoustic-trawl survey (ATS) sample sizes use the
integer values aligned with the modified ADMB model. Age-1 survey selectivity
remains separately parameterized from the age-2--15 curve, and each likelihood
contribution evaluates the complete 15-age composition. Compositions use the
supported `MultinomialAFSC` likelihood. We added a robustness constant of
0.001 to both observed and expected proportions before evaluating the
likelihood. This prevents `log(0)` and limits the influence of observations in
bins with expected proportions near zero.

The run uses Rceattle version
`r model_lineage$Value[model_lineage$Item == "Rceattle version"]` from
upstream commit
`r substr(model_lineage$Value[model_lineage$Item == "Rceattle upstream commit"], 1, 12)`,
with the model configuration synchronized to `Rceattle-models` commit
`r substr(model_lineage$Value[model_lineage$Item == "Rceattle-models upstream commit"], 1, 12)`.

The next-assessment update script review is complete, and execution
awaits complete new-year observations. The script
duplicates terminal records and places placeholders for new catch,
composition, and survey observations. The script serves as a template until
complete new-year observations are available; after population, it creates a
complete assessment workbook.

### Selectivity

The configuration uses `NonParametricPM` fishery selectivity with annual
deviations. When fit to the data, the model reached a small maximum gradient.
The Hessian condition number was approximately 489,000 and received `OK`
status. Its least-identified direction remained concentrated in
`sel_coff_dev`, specifically the shared ATS/AVO block rather than the shared
fishery/CPUE block.

The time-varying selectivity penalties use explicit standard deviations
on log-selectivity random-walk increments. The fishery and its shared
CPUE selectivity block use an SD of 0.500, ATS and AVO use 0.138, and BTS
uses 1.000. ATS and AVO also use a direct coefficient-increment penalty
(`Sel_curve_pen3 = 0.1`) to constrain the across-age common-mode direction
that is removed by annual selectivity normalization. The
fishery specification also retains the ADMB-matched curve-shape penalty
weights (12.5, 1/60, and 1) and an average-selectivity centering weight
of 10. These values are penalty coefficients rather than SDs.

The fitting sequence, composition-likelihood sensitivity, and 2D age-by-year
AR1 development work are documented in the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: fig-selectivity-ridges
#| fig-cap: "Relative fishery selectivity by year for the ADMB model and Rceattle configuration. Each annual curve is normalized to a maximum of one."
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side ridge plots show relative fishery selectivity at ages 1 through 15 for years 1964 through 2024 for the ADMB model and Rceattle configuration."
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

ggplot(
  selectivity_ridges |>
    filter(Model %in% c("ADMB reference", "Rceattle NonParametricPM")),
  aes(
    x = Age,
    y = Year_factor,
    height = Relative_selectivity,
    fill = Model
  )
) +
  ggridges::geom_ridgeline(
    scale = 3.8,
    alpha = 0.28,
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.2,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Model), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "ADMB reference" = "#1f78b4",
    "Rceattle NonParametricPM" = "#1b9e77"
  )) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(1, 15), breaks = 1:15) +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Year") +
  ggthemes::theme_few() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.spacing.x = grid::unit(1.2, "lines")
  )
```

## ADMB Comparison Results

When the Rceattle parameters and fishery selectivity are set to the ADMB values,
the two programs give nearly identical population calculations. Mean absolute
differences are
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "SSB mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for spawning biomass and
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Catch mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for predicted catch. Annual Rceattle-to-ADMB ratios for both quantities remain
extremely close to one (@fig-admb-parameter-comparison).

The reported Rceattle likelihood contributions are
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Rceattle reported index negative log-likelihood"])`
for indices,
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Rceattle reported catch negative log-likelihood"])`
for catch,
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Rceattle reported composition negative log-likelihood"])`
for age compositions, and
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Rceattle reported recruitment-deviation negative log-likelihood"])`
for recruitment deviations. Their sum is
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Rceattle reported likelihood-component sum"])`.
The ADMB `tot_like` and `dat_like` values are
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "ADMB total negative log-likelihood (tot_like; not directly comparable)"])`
and
`r sprintf("%.3f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "ADMB data negative log-likelihood (dat_like; not directly comparable)"])`,
respectively, but cannot be compared directly because the two programs include
different likelihood terms, penalties, and constants. The ADMB maximum absolute
gradient is
`r scientific(fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "ADMB maximum gradient component"], digits = 3)`;
no Rceattle model-parameter gradient is available from this comparison because
Rceattle does not estimate parameters in this run.

```{r}
#| label: fig-admb-parameter-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Rceattle-to-ADMB ratios for spawning biomass and predicted catch when Rceattle uses the ADMB parameter values."
#| fig-alt: "Two time-series panels show Rceattle divided by ADMB for spawning biomass and predicted catch from 1964 through 2024. Both lines remain extremely close to one."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5

ggplot(fixed_parameter_ratio_long, aes(x = Year, y = Ratio)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2, color = "gray45") +
  geom_line(color = "#1b9e77", linewidth = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Quantity), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.000001)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Rceattle / ADMB") +
  ggthemes::theme_few()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fitted-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between fitted Rceattle trajectories and the modified ADMB reference. Correlation is the Pearson correlation across annual estimates. Mean absolute (%) and maximum absolute (%) are the average and largest absolute annual percentage differences, respectively. The 2024 difference (%) is the signed terminal-year difference of Rceattle relative to ADMB; negative values indicate that the Rceattle estimate is lower."
#| tbl-pos: H

comparison_summary |>
  filter(Method == "Rceattle configuration") |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Method") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(

    ),

  ) |>

  ) |>

    Quantity ~ px(150),
    Correlation ~ px(90),
    everything() ~ px(110)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectories
#| fig-cap: "ADMB and fitted Rceattle trajectories for spawning biomass, recruitment, and total biomass. The Rceattle series is from the fit in which its parameters were estimated."
#| fig-alt: "Three vertically stacked time-series panels compare ADMB estimates with estimates from the fitted Rceattle model for spawning biomass, recruitment, and total biomass from 1964 through 2024."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8

ggplot(
  quantity_long |>
    filter(Method %in% c("ADMB reference", "Rceattle NonParametricPM")) |>
    mutate(
      Method = recode(
        as.character(Method),

      )
    ),
  aes(x = Year, y = Value, color = Method, linetype = Method)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Quantity), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +

    "ADMB reference" = "#1b9e77",
    "Rceattle fit (parameters estimated)" = "#d95f02"
  )) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(
    "ADMB reference" = "22",

```

When Rceattle estimates its parameters, the fitted trajectories differ most
from ADMB during the early period and in the terminal recruitment estimate
(@fig-trajectories). These trajectories are distinct from the run in which
Rceattle parameters are set to the ADMB values. The fitted trajectories remain
highly correlated with the ADMB reference, with relatively small mean annual
differences (@tbl-fitted-comparison). Development sensitivities are documented
in the appendix.

The Rceattle fit has a small maximum gradient and a positive-definite Hessian.
Adding the direct ATS/AVO coefficient-increment penalty reduced the condition
number from approximately 1.14 million to 489,000 and removed the prior
Hessian-conditioning warning. The residual weakest direction remains almost
entirely in the shared time-varying ATS/AVO selectivity coefficients, not the
fishery/CPUE coefficients, so this block remains an appropriate focus for
sensitivity checks even though the formal warning is resolved.

## Diagnostics

The numerical convergence checks for the fitted Rceattle model, including the
objective, maximum gradient, and Hessian status, indicated convergence
(@tbl-convergence). The fit and status of the other diagnostic products are
provided in @tbl-diagnostic-status.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-convergence
#| tbl-cap: "Stored Rceattle convergence checks for the evaluated configurations."
#| tbl-pos: H

convergence_summary |>
  filter(Model == "Rceattle fit") |>
  select(
    Model,
    Status,
    Objective,
    Max_gradient,
    Worst_parameter,
    Positive_definite_Hessian
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Objective, Max_gradient), decimals = 6) |>
  cols_label(
    Max_gradient = "Max gradient",
    Worst_parameter = "Weakest component",
    Positive_definite_Hessian = "PD Hessian"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    Model ~ px(135),
    Status ~ px(65),
    Objective ~ px(95),
    Max_gradient ~ px(95),
    Worst_parameter ~ px(105),
    Positive_definite_Hessian ~ px(80)
  )
```

```{r}
diagnostic_status |>
```

### Rceattle 5.8.1 self-test validation

Rceattle 5.8.1 changed simulation of natural-scale normal and multivariate
normal survey indices. The fitted likelihood remains an untruncated normal;
the simulator redraws non-positive values because `data_check()` excludes
them. The resulting self-test therefore uses a normal distribution truncated
at zero whenever rejection occurs.

The ADMB-to-Rceattle comparison was rerun first with Rceattle 5.8.1. Its saved
summary gives mean absolute differences of
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "SSB mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for spawning biomass and
`r sprintf("%.6f", fixed_parameter_summary$Value[fixed_parameter_summary$Metric == "Catch mean absolute percent difference"])`%
for predicted catch. This confirms that the package update preserved the
agreement in the population calculations.

The self-test uses the same delivered EBS workbook and supported
`MultinomialAFSC` composition criterion as the Rceattle configuration. The
observed-data fit reproduced the stored
objective of 716.948070, maximum gradient of 0.000041, and `OK` status with a
positive-definite Hessian. The Hessian condition number was approximately
$4.9 \times 10^5$; its least-identified direction remained concentrated in the
shared ATS/AVO `sel_coff_dev` block rather than fishery/CPUE.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rceattle-581-self-test
#| tbl-cap: "Rceattle 5.8.1 self-test and paired-restart validation for the upstream-supported EBS configuration."

rceattle_581_validation |>
  mutate(
    Value = case_when(
      grepl("difference|probability", Metric, ignore.case = TRUE) ~
        format(Value, digits = 6, scientific = TRUE),
      grepl("bias", Metric, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ sprintf("%.3f%%", Value),
      TRUE ~ format(Value, trim = TRUE)
    )
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_width(Metric ~ px(520), Value ~ px(150))
```

All 50 phased simulations converged with `OK` status when refitted from the
original initial values. Repeating the same simulated datasets from the fitted
parameter values also produced 50 `OK` fits. Paired objectives agreed within
$3.1 \times 10^{-8}$, so these simulations showed no start-dependent mode.
Median spawning-biomass bias was -1.06% across years and -0.91% in the terminal
year. These results validate the revised self-test workflow; they do not rule
out the mode previously encountered when fitting the observed data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rceattle-581-truncation
#| tbl-cap: "Fleet-level probability of a non-positive index draw under the fitted, untruncated observation distribution."

rceattle_581_truncation |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(
    columns = c(
      Maximum_nonpositive_probability,
      Mean_nonpositive_probability
    ),
    decimals = 2
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Fleet_name = "Fleet",
    Fleet_code = "Code",
    Index_distribution = "Distribution",
    Maximum_nonpositive_probability = "Maximum row probability",
    Mean_nonpositive_probability = "Mean row probability",
    Rows_above_2_percent = "Rows above 2%"
  )
```

One AVO row had a 3.76% non-positive probability and one BTS multivariate-normal
row had a 6.67% probability. Those rows exceed the package's 2% warning
threshold and should be identified when interpreting recovery. CPUE and the
remaining index series had negligible or zero marginal rejection probability.

### OSA Residuals

OSA residuals run on the Rceattle configuration. The aggregate composition
fits are generally close, while all three OSA quantile plots are narrower than
the standard-normal reference (@fig-osa). These diagnostics apply to the fitted
`NonParametricPM` selectivity configuration. The failed 2D-AR1 sensitivity and
ADMB-to-Rceattle calculation use separate results. The composition diagnostics use `afscOSA` version
`r as.character(utils::packageVersion("afscOSA"))` and pass Rceattle's
internally calculated residuals to `afscOSA::run_osa()`. The residual builder
uses complete ages 1--15, with nominal fishery sample sizes and the integer
BTS and ATS sample sizes aligned with the modified ADMB model. This follows
the current [afscOSA interpretation
guidance](https://noaa-afsc.github.io/afscOSA/#interpretation-and-use-of-diagnostics)
while retaining Rceattle's residual calculation.

Following that guidance, the aggregate age-composition fits are the first check for systematic
misfit, including patterns that could indicate an unsuitable selectivity
form. The red vertical ranges contain 95% of data simulated from the
fitted multinomial model conditional on the aggregate sample size and
estimated parameter values held constant. They represent conditional simulation
variability. The quantile--quantile
plots then assess whether the OSA residuals resemble a standard normal
distribution. The standard deviation of normalized residuals (SDNR)
should be near one, and the displayed tail statistics provide a separate
check on extreme residual behavior. Finally, the OSA and Pearson bubble
plots are used to look for age, year, or cohort patterns that may suggest
the source of misfit. Each statistic and nominal interval contributes to
an integrated diagnostic interpretation rather than an automatic
model-rejection rule.

```{r}
#| label: fig-osa
#| fig-cap: "Age-composition diagnostics for the Rceattle fit. The fit uses complete ages 1--15, nominal fishery sample sizes, and BTS and ATS integer sample sizes aligned with the modified ADMB model. Diagnostics were produced with afscOSA for the fishery, bottom trawl survey (BTS), and acoustic-trawl survey (ATS). The top row compares aggregate observed proportions (blue bars) with fitted proportions (red points and lines); red vertical ranges contain 95% of data simulated conditionally from the fitted multinomial model, aggregate sample size, and estimated parameter values held constant. The second row shows quantile--quantile plots of Rceattle's internal one-step-ahead (OSA) residuals with the standard deviation of normalized residuals (SDNR), its expected 95% interval, and lower and upper tail diagnostics. The lower rows show OSA and Pearson residuals by age and year; red and blue indicate positive and negative residuals, and bubble area represents magnitude. Absolute residuals greater than 6 are capped at 6 for display. The fitted model retains ATS 2020; its sample size of one yields zero rounded counts in the afscOSA plotting conversion, so the plotting layer omits that row."
#| fig-alt: "Four rows of age-composition diagnostics in columns for the fishery, bottom trawl survey, and acoustic-trawl survey. Aggregate fits are generally close. All three OSA quantile plots are narrower than the standard-normal reference, with SDNR values below one. Bubble plots show age- and year-related residual patterns."
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 13

osa_panels <- afscOSA::plot_osa(
  afscosa_composition,
  plot = FALSE,
  use_agg_proportions = TRUE,
  figheight = 13,
  figwidth = 12
)

osa_panels$aggcomp <- osa_panels$aggcomp +
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_size = 10)
osa_panels$qq <- osa_panels$qq +
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_size = 10)
osa_panels$bubble <- osa_panels$bubble +
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.box.spacing = grid::unit(0, "pt"),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 0, b = 0, unit = "pt"),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = -5, r = 0, b = 0, l = 0, unit = "pt")
  )
osa_panels$bubble_pearson <- osa_panels$bubble_pearson +
  ggthemes::theme_few(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

cowplot::plot_grid(
  osa_panels$aggcomp,
  osa_panels$qq,
  osa_panels$bubble,
  osa_panels$bubble_pearson,
  nrow = 4,
  rel_heights = c(5, 5, 4.5, 4)
)
```

The aggregate observed and fitted compositions are generally close,
although the survey panels contain some age-specific departures. The
OSA distributions are narrower than the standard-normal reference for
all three composition sources: SDNR is
`r sprintf("%.2f", osa_table$sdnr[osa_table$Data_group == "Fishery comp"])`
for the fishery,
`r sprintf("%.2f", osa_table$sdnr[osa_table$Data_group == "BTS comp"])`
for BTS, and
`r sprintf("%.2f", osa_table$sdnr[osa_table$Data_group == "ATS comp"])`
for ATS. Their tail diagnostics also show shorter-than-expected tails.
Together these results indicate underdispersion relative to the fitted
multinomial observation model. Model selection requires this information
alongside the full suite of diagnostics. The bubble
plots should instead be used to identify persistent age, year, or cohort
patterns and to guide focused checks of selectivity, composition
weighting, and observation-model assumptions. One Pearson residual
(8.86) is capped at 6 in the figure, following the package's plotting
convention.

### Retrospective patterns

Nine retrospective peels were run from the Rceattle fit. The unpeeled model ends in `r terminal_year`, and
the peeled fits end in `r terminal_year - 1` through
`r terminal_year - 9`. Each peel preserves the data-availability pattern
of the 2024 model. Thus, fishery age compositions end one year before
the peel terminal year, survey series retain their historical sampling
schedule and terminal lags, and earlier discontinued series retain their
original ending years.

Each peel applies the fitting sequence documented in the appendix. The
terminal-year fishery and mirrored catch-per-unit-effort selectivity
increments are fixed at zero. All nine final fits received
`OK` convergence status, with maximum gradients from
`r scientific(min(retro_convergence$Maximum_gradient[retro_convergence$Terminal_year < terminal_year]), digits = 2)`
to
`r scientific(max(retro_convergence$Maximum_gradient[retro_convergence$Terminal_year < terminal_year]), digits = 2)`.

The NonParametricPM fishery selectivity is parameterized at age. The base
`sel_coff` parameters and annual `sel_coff_dev` random-walk increments apply
to age bins; the fishery uses `r fishery_selectivity_bins` estimated bins and
holds older ages at the last estimated value. Fixing every terminal-year increment at zero therefore
holds the realized terminal selectivity-at-age curve at the preceding-year
curve. Across all peels and both the fishery and mirrored catch-per-unit-effort
series, the maximum absolute terminal-to-preceding-year difference was
`r scientific(retro_terminal_selectivity_max_difference, digits = 2)`.
These Rceattle fits are separate from the legacy AD Model Builder (ADMB)
retrospective files.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rceattle-retrospectives
#| fig-cap: "Nine retrospective peels for the Rceattle configuration. The black line is the unpeeled model ending in 2024; colored lines are successive peels ending in 2023 through 2015 and are plotted through each peel's terminal year. Each peel preserves the original data-availability lags and fixes the terminal fishery/CPUE selectivity-at-age increment at zero, holding the terminal curve at its preceding-year value. All nine fits received OK convergence status."
#| fig-alt: "Faceted line plots of spawning biomass, total biomass, recruitment, and fishing mortality for the 2024 Rceattle fit and nine retrospective peels. The peeled trajectories show moderate systematic departures from the base fit, especially for spawning biomass."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

retro_plot_data <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(retro_models), function(i) {
  model <- retro_models[[i]]
  end_year <- retro_terminal_years[i]
  model_years <- seq(model$data_list$styr, end_year)
  n <- length(model_years)
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      Year = model_years,
      Value = as.numeric(model$quantities$ssb[1, seq_len(n)]),
      Quantity = "Spawning biomass"
    ),
    tibble(
      Year = model_years,
      Value = as.numeric(model$quantities$biomass[1, seq_len(n)]),
      Quantity = "Total biomass"
    ),
    tibble(
      Year = model_years,
      Value = as.numeric(model$quantities$R[1, seq_len(n)]),
      Quantity = "Recruitment"
    ),
    tibble(
      Year = model_years,
      Value = as.numeric(model$quantities$F_spp[1, seq_len(n)]),
      Quantity = "Fishing mortality"
    )
  ) |>
    mutate(
      Terminal_year = factor(end_year, levels = sort(retro_terminal_years)),
      Series = if_else(end_year == terminal_year, "Base", "Peel")
    )
}))

ggplot(retro_plot_data, aes(Year, Value, group = Terminal_year)) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(retro_plot_data, Series == "Peel"),
    aes(color = Terminal_year),
    linewidth = 0.65,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(retro_plot_data, Series == "Base"),
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Quantity), scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "C", end = 0.9, direction = -1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Terminal year") +
  ggthemes::theme_few() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rceattle-mohns-rho
#| tbl-cap: "Mohn's rho for the nine retrospective peels of the Rceattle configuration. Values are the mean relative difference between a peeled estimate in its terminal year and the corresponding estimate from the unpeeled model. Each peel preserves the 2024 data-availability pattern and fixes the terminal fishery/CPUE selectivity-at-age increment at zero."

retro_mohns |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = `Mohn's rho`, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = Quantity) |>
  cols_align(align = "right", columns = c(Peels, `Mohn's rho`))
```

The estimated Mohn's rho values are
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Spawning biomass"])`
for spawning biomass,
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Total biomass"])`
for total biomass,
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Recruitment"])`
for recruitment, and
`r sprintf("%.3f", retro_mohns[["Mohn's rho"]][retro_mohns$Quantity == "Fishing mortality"])`
for fishing mortality. The positive biomass and recruitment values
indicate that the peeled models generally estimate higher quantities at
their terminal years than the corresponding unpeeled estimates. The
negative fishing-mortality value indicates lower terminal fishing
mortality in the peels. Spawning biomass shows the largest average
relative difference. The consistent `OK` statuses and small gradients
support interpretation of these values as properties of the revised
retrospective specification, while the magnitude of spawning-biomass
rho motivates continued evaluation of selectivity, survey influence,
and recent recruitment estimates.

## Projections

The saved Rceattle fit supplies every population and
fishery input for the Standard Projection Model calculations implemented in
`spmR` [@ianelli2026spmR]. The run uses `spmR` version 0.3.0 from pinned
main-branch commit `e86fc6aa`. The adapter in
`R/write_spmr_projection_inputs.R` writes terminal abundance, natural
mortality, maturity, spawning and fishery weights, the arithmetic mean of
fishery selectivity-at-age over the most recent five assessment years
(2020--2024), recruitment, and spawning-biomass histories to `pm.prj`. The
same five years define the recent average fishing mortality. The reproducible
runner `R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R` then applies those inputs to all seven
Tier 3 alternatives. The report reads the saved projection products, so every
table and figure in this section comes from the same saved Rceattle fit. The
complete field mapping and validation sequence are documented in Appendix A-2.

```{r}
#| label: spmr-projection-products
#| include: false
projection_dir <- project_file(params$projection_dir)
projection_alt2_dir <- project_file(params$projection_alt2_dir)
spmr_manifest <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "manifest.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_lineage <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "lineage.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_age_schedules <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "age_schedules.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_selectivity_history <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "fishery_selectivity_recent_years.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_detail <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "spm_detail.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_alt2_detail <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_alt2_dir, "spm_detail.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE
)
spmr_alt_desc <- tibble(
  Alternative = 1:7,
  Name = c(
    "Maximum permissible ABC", "Author-specified ABC", "Average recent F",
    "Alternative SPR rate", "No fishing", "OFL threshold determination",
    "Status-determination ramp"
  ),
  Description = c(
    "Maximum permissible Tier 3 ABC harvest rate.",
    "Author-specified adjustment to the Tier 3 ABC harvest rate; the current multiplier is 1.0.",
    "Recent average fishing mortality from the Rceattle-derived input file.",
    "User-specified SPR rate of 0.60.",
    "Zero fishing mortality after the fixed-catch years.",
    "OFL harvest rate for threshold and status-determination calculations.",
    "Maximum permissible ABC for three years followed by the OFL status-determination calculation."
  )
)
```

### Seven Tier 3 Scenario Results

Catches for 2025 and 2026 are fixed at 1,350 thousand t in every alternative;
the alternatives therefore first diverge in 2027
(@tbl-spmr-tier3-seven-scenarios). The reported values are simulation means
from 1,000 SPM simulations.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spmr-tier3-seven-scenarios
#| tbl-cap: 'Tier 3 projection results for all seven FMP alternatives using inputs generated from the Rceattle EBS pollock model. Catch and biomass quantities are in thousand t; B/B~35%~ is spawning biomass relative to the Tier 3 B~35%~ proxy.'
#| tbl-pos: "H"
readr::read_csv(
  file.path(projection_dir, "tier3_seven_scenario_table.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(Alt, Scenario),
    names_to = c(".value", "Year"),
    names_pattern = "(.+)_(\\d{4})"
  ) |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year)) |>
  rename(`B/B35` = B_B35) |>
  arrange(Alt, Year) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Catch, ABC, OFL, SSB), decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(columns = F, decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `B/B35`, decimals = 2) |>
  cols_width(
    Alt ~ px(35),
    Scenario ~ px(175),
    Year ~ px(45),
    c(Catch, ABC, OFL, SSB) ~ px(58),
    F ~ px(45),
    `B/B35` ~ px(55)
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(8)) |>
  tab_header(title = "Seven Tier 3 Projection Alternatives")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spmr-projection-age-schedules
#| tbl-cap: "Age-specific schedules applied in SPM. Natural mortality, maturity, and weights come from the terminal Rceattle configuration; fishery selectivity is the arithmetic mean at age over 2020--2024."
#| tbl-pos: "H"
spmr_age_schedules |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = -Age, decimals = 3) |>
  tab_header(title = "Projection Age-Specific Schedules")
```

### Alternative 2 Fixed-Catch Projection

This additional run applies Alternative 2 and fixes catch at 1,300 thousand t
for 2025--2032. The projection horizon includes every fixed-catch year.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-spmr-alt2-fixed-results
#| tbl-cap: 'Candidate ABC projection given assumed future catches. Catch is fixed at 1,300 thousand t; ABC is the maximum permissible ABC calculated by SPM. B/B~35%~ is mean spawning biomass relative to the Tier 3 proxy.'
spmr_alt2_detail |>
  filter(Alt == 2) |>

```


### Projection Figures

The figures summarize the 1,000 simulations for each alternative. Lines show
simulation medians and ribbons show central 90% intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spmr-projection-stock-status
#| fig-cap: "Projected spawning biomass under all seven Tier 3 alternatives. Lines are simulation medians, ribbons span the 5th to 95th percentiles, and dashed lines mark B35%."
#| fig-alt: "Seven-panel chart of projected spawning biomass. Each panel shows a median trajectory, a central 90-percent interval, and the B35-percent reference line for one Tier 3 alternative."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
spmr_alt_names <- setNames(
  paste0("Alt ", spmr_alt_desc$Alternative, ": ", spmr_alt_desc$Name),
  spmr_alt_desc$Alternative
)
spmr_plot_data <- spmr_detail |>
  mutate(Scenario = factor(spmr_alt_names[as.character(Alt)], levels = spmr_alt_names))
spmr_plot_data |>
  group_by(Scenario, Year) |>
  summarize(
    Lower = quantile(SSB, 0.05), Median = median(SSB), Upper = quantile(SSB, 0.95),
    B35 = first(B35), .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, Median)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), fill = "#2b7a9b", alpha = 0.22) +
  geom_line(color = "#102f3d", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_line(aes(y = B35), color = "#4d4d4d", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(Scenario), ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Spawning biomass (thousand t)") +
  ggthemes::theme_few()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-spmr-projection-removals
#| fig-cap: "Projected catch, ABC, and OFL under all seven Tier 3 alternatives. Lines are simulation medians and catch ribbons span the 5th to 95th percentiles."
#| fig-alt: "Seven-panel chart of projected removals. Each panel compares median catch, ABC, and OFL trajectories and shows the central 90-percent interval for catch."
#| fig-width: 10

removal_summary <- spmr_plot_data |>
  select(Scenario, Year, Catch, ABC, OFL) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Catch, ABC, OFL), names_to = "Quantity", values_to = "Value") |>
  group_by(Scenario, Year, Quantity) |>
  summarize(
    Lower = quantile(Value, 0.05), Median = median(Value), Upper = quantile(Value, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(removal_summary, aes(Year, Median, linetype = Quantity)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = filter(removal_summary, Quantity == "Catch"),
    mapping = aes(x = Year, ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "#5b8c5a", alpha = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "#102f3d", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Scenario), ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Thousand metric tons", linetype = "Quantity") +
  ggthemes::theme_few()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-spmr-projection-fishing-mortality
#| fig-cap: "Projected fishing mortality under all seven Tier 3 alternatives. Lines are simulation medians and ribbons span the 5th to 95th percentiles."
#| fig-alt: "Seven-panel chart of projected fishing mortality. Each panel shows the median trajectory and central 90-percent interval for one Tier 3 alternative."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
spmr_plot_data |>
  group_by(Scenario, Year) |>
  summarize(
    Lower = quantile(F, 0.05), Median = median(F), Upper = quantile(F, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(Year, Median)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = Lower, ymax = Upper), fill = "#d18b2c", alpha = 0.24) +
  geom_line(color = "#4d3210", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(vars(Scenario), ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Fishing mortality") +
  ggthemes::theme_few()
```

## Exploratory DSEM Recruitment Pathways

This section is the indicator-analysis pilot within a draft EBS pollock
Ecosystem and Socioeconomic Profile (ESP), rather than an attempt to estimate
the full pollock early-survival system. The BSAI Groundfish Plan Team
recommended in 2021 that an EBS walleye pollock ESP be added to the list of
future ESPs [@npfmc2021bsai]. The analysis follows the
sequence recommended in the AFSC causal-modeling guidance: define the outcome,
build a literature-based mechanism table and generic DAG, select a small set of
scientifically defensible graphs, retain a no-edge baseline, and compare all
graphs on the same data [@monnahan2026causalpractices]. The mechanism table and
DAG draw on the January 2025 pollock workshop, the age-0 pollock working-group
material, and the Tiger Team data-availability synthesis
[@monnahan2026pollockworkshop; @siddon2026age0pollock; @afsc2026age0dag;
@ianelli2026tigerteam] and the
[EBS pollock Early Survival Pathways synthesis](https://afsc-assessments.github.io/ebswp_esp/)
[@ianelli2026ebswpesp].

The response is the Rceattle age-1 recruitment state. The two examples test
late-summer SST in the cohort's age-0 year and cold-pool extent in the following
age-1 calendar year. They were selected because both have relatively long
annual records and represent distinct, prespecified hypotheses. The analysis
does not treat them as direct measurements of prey quality, energetic
condition, cannibalism, or survival.

### ESP development scope

The September product documents the justification, synthesis, generic DAG,
mechanism table, and two illustrative fits. It does not substitute a long list
of available covariates for a small set of causal hypotheses. The intended
progression to November is summarized in @tbl-esp-development-scope; the full
draft ESP structure is provided in Appendix A-3.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-esp-development-scope
#| tbl-cap: "Development scope for the EBS pollock ESP and its Rceattle-DSEM indicator analysis."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

tibble::tribble(

  "Justification and outcome", "Document the Plan Team request and define age-1 recruitment as the focal population response.", "Confirm the focal response and management use with the ESP team.",

  "Indicator analysis", "Compare the two single-edge examples and their combined diagnostic with the no-edge IID reference.", "Add predictive, retrospective, timing, and observation-error checks to the candidate-DAG comparison.",
  "Management use", "Use results to illustrate the integrated Rceattle-DSEM workflow and identify data gaps.", "Determine whether validated indicators are suitable for operational recruitment modeling or risk-table context."
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    September_draft = "September draft",
    November_target = "November target"
  ) |>
  cols_width(
    Component ~ px(135),
```

### Mechanism table and generic DAG

The reduced mechanism table distinguishes processes that can be tested with the
current annual data from biologically important mediators that remain
intermittent or unavailable (@tbl-dsem-mechanisms). Expected signs describe the
direction from the listed driver toward age-1 recruitment, whether directly or
through the stated mechanism.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-mechanisms
#| tbl-cap: "Reduced mechanism table for the illustrative age-0 to age-1 recruitment analysis. Coverage refers to the cohort-aligned data presently available to this working paper."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

tibble::tribble(
  ~Driver, ~Mechanism, ~Expected_sign, ~Current_coverage, ~Role_in_this_section,
  "Sea ice", "Winter ice affects summer cold-pool extent, bloom conditions, and prey production.", "Indirect", "Annual physical index available; not fitted here", "Upstream context",

  "Age-0 late-summer SST", "Warmer water can increase metabolic demand and reduce energy stored before winter.", "Negative", sprintf("%d annual values", sum(is.finite(dsem_covariates$LateSummerSST))), "Illustrative proxy edge",
  "Large copepods and euphausiids", "Lipid-rich prey supports age-0 growth, energy storage, and overwinter survival.", "Positive", "Intermittent; 15 values in the current ESP cohort table", "Unfitted mediator",
  "Fall age-0 energy", "Higher energy density and total energy increase overwinter survival to age 1.", "Positive", "Absent from the current annual cohort table", "Priority mediator",
  "Adult-pollock overlap", "Greater adult-juvenile overlap increases cannibalism exposure.", "Negative", "A separate range-overlap product exists, but its survey timing is contemporaneous with the age-1 state", "Deferred from the main example"
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_width(
    Driver ~ px(90),
    Mechanism ~ px(205),
    Expected_sign ~ px(65),

  ) |>
  cols_label(
    Expected_sign = "Expected sign",
    Current_coverage = "Current coverage",
    Role_in_this_section = "Role here"
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(8))
```

The generic DAG is adapted from the age-0 pollock working-group graph and
retains both bottom-up and top-down routes (@fig-dsem-dag). It makes the
unobserved or intermittent mediators visible instead of allowing the two
available physical proxies to stand in for entire mechanisms. Solid arrows are
conceptual. Dashed arrows are the only recruitment paths fitted in this proof
of concept.

```{mermaid}

Dashed arrows connect late-summer SST and cold-pool extent directly to recruitment for the two illustrative fitted hypotheses."

```

The generic graph is intentionally broader than the statistical examples. It
shows that a negative SST coefficient would be consistent with an energetic
constraint, but would not identify prey quality, age-0 energy, or overwinter
survival as the active mediator. Likewise, a cold-pool coefficient would be a
proxy for spatial separation and cannibalism unless overlap and mortality were
observed directly.

### Two illustrative hypotheses

The proof of concept compares two single-edge hypotheses with a common
reference:

- **Energetic-condition proxy:** higher age-0 late-summer SST is associated
  with lower age-1 recruitment because warmer conditions can increase
  metabolic demand and reduce fall energy reserves
  [@heintz2013; @siddon2013; @duffyanderson2016].
- **Spatial-separation proxy:** larger cold-pool extent is associated with
  higher age-1 recruitment because it can reduce juvenile-adult spatial
  overlap and cannibalism.

The age-0 SST value is carried forward to the DSEM row for that cohort's age-1
recruitment. The zero-lag path is therefore cohort-aligned rather than a claim
that SST was measured in the age-1 year. In this section "IID" refers to the
no-recruitment-edge reference model. The combined model is retained as a
limited diagnostic of whether the two proxy edges add information when fitted
together; it is not a third mechanistic hypothesis.

All four specifications use the same observation-year universe, missingness
pattern, standardization, and AR(1) processes for the observed covariates.
Within this common data block, AIC compares relative fit after accounting for
model complexity. The percentage reduction in residual recruitment variation
compares each model's estimated unexplained recruitment variance with the IID
reference. It is an in-sample description, not a causal R-squared or a
predictive-skill score.

### Illustrative results

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-model-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative Rceattle-DSEM model comparison. Delta AIC and the percentage reduction in residual recruitment variation are calculated within the common observation block."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

dsem_summary |>
  select(
    Model,
    AIC,
    `Delta AIC`,
    `Residual variation reduced (%)`
  ) |>
  arrange(AIC) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(AIC, `Delta AIC`), decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = `Residual variation reduced (%)`, decimals = 1) |>
  cols_width(
    Model ~ px(190),
    `Residual variation reduced (%)` ~ px(130),
    everything() ~ px(95)
  )
```

All four fits reached `OK` status, had positive-definite Hessians, and had
maximum absolute gradients no larger than
`r format(max(dsem_summary$maximum_gradient), scientific = TRUE, digits = 2)`.
The age-0 late-summer SST model had the lowest AIC
(@tbl-dsem-model-comparison; @fig-dsem-aic) and reduced estimated residual
recruitment variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "late_summer_sst"])`%
relative to IID. The cold-pool-only model reduced residual variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "cold_pool"])`%
and had higher AIC than IID. The combined model reduced residual variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "combined"])`%,
but its additional parameter left its AIC above the SST-only model.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dsem-aic
#| fig-cap: "Akaike information criterion differences for the illustrative DSEM models. The age-0 late-summer SST model has the lowest AIC."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal bars compare delta AIC for the no-edge IID reference, cold pool, age-0 late-summer SST, and the combined proxy model. The SST-only model has the lowest AIC, followed by the combined model, IID, and cold-pool-only model."
#| out-width: "76%"
#| fig-align: center

knitr::include_graphics(dsem_aic_figure_file)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dsem-recruitment-paths
#| tbl-cap: "Standardized proxy paths to age-1 recruitment. Intervals are the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors."
#| tbl-pos: "H"

dsem_recruitment_paths |>
  select(Model, Covariate, estimate, standard_error, lower_95, upper_95) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "Model") |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(estimate, standard_error, lower_95, upper_95),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  cols_label(
    estimate = "Estimate",
    standard_error = "Standard error",
    lower_95 = "Lower 95%",
    upper_95 = "Upper 95%"
  )
```

The SST coefficient was negative and its interval excluded zero in both the
single-edge and combined models. The cold-pool coefficient was small and its
interval included zero in both models (@tbl-dsem-recruitment-paths;
@fig-dsem-edges). In plain language, the current annual data contain a modest
in-sample association consistent with the warm-year energetic-constraint
hypothesis, while the direct cold-pool proxy edge received little support.
Neither result establishes the intervening mechanism.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dsem-edges
#| fig-cap: "Standardized coefficients for the illustrative DSEM models. Points are estimates and horizontal lines are 95% intervals. Blue edges describe temporal persistence in observed covariates; orange edges are the two direct proxy paths to age-1 recruitment."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels show standardized DSEM coefficients. Both environmental series have positive temporal persistence. Age-0 late-summer SST has a negative recruitment coefficient with its interval below zero, while the cold-pool recruitment coefficient is close to zero and its interval overlaps zero."
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(dsem_edges_figure_file)
```

The missingness-preserving randomization check replaced both environmental
series with independent standard-normal values using seed
`r sprintf("%d", as.integer(dsem_random_design$seed))`. None of the randomized
recruitment paths improved on the randomized IID model: their delta AIC values
ranged from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(dsem_random_summary[["Delta AIC"]][dsem_random_summary$model != "iid"]))`
to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(dsem_random_summary[["Delta AIC"]][dsem_random_summary$model != "iid"]))`,
and every randomized path interval included zero. This is a basic check against
an identical signal arising from arbitrary series with the same gaps; it does
not replace out-of-sample validation.

### Interpretation and next test

This proof of concept supports keeping the candidate set small. The SST result
is useful as an illustration of the Rceattle-DSEM connection, but SST is an
upstream proxy. The next scientifically stronger test is to insert a proximal
mediator from the mechanism table: fall age-0 total energy or energy density,
followed by a lipid-rich large-copepod/euphausiid index when enough cohort years
are available [@eisner2020copepods; @heintz2013; @siddon2013]. That sequence
would test whether the SST association weakens when the hypothesized energetic
path is represented directly.

A top-down overlap example should return only after its timing and uncertainty
are aligned with the age-0-to-age-1 survival interval. The available
adult-pollock overlap product is informative, but its survey occurs after the
start-of-year age-1 state and it is partly population-derived. Including it here
would blur a causal example with a contemporaneous association.

Before either proxy is considered for operational recruitment inference, the
paths should be tested with terminal-year or blocked prediction, retrospective
stability, alternative cohort timing, and observation-error sensitivity.
These DSEM results remain separate from the assessment configuration and
projection results.

## Summary

When Rceattle parameters and fishery selectivity are set to the values used in
the ADMB model, Rceattle reproduces spawning
biomass and predicted catch to numerical precision. This establishes
agreement in the tested population-dynamics calculations and parameter
mapping. When Rceattle is fit to the data, the trajectories differ more,
and the residual least-identified direction remains in the shared ATS/AVO
annual selectivity deviations. The added ATS/AVO coefficient-increment penalty
reduced the condition number below the convergence-warning threshold.

The diagnostic results identify a focused development path for the September
2026 Plan Team evaluation. The Rceattle fit reaches a small gradient,
an `OK` convergence status, and a positive-definite Hessian. Composition OSA
residuals remain underdispersed.
Nine terminal-year-consistent peels converge successfully and produce
positive retrospective bias in spawning biomass, total biomass, and
recruitment, together with negative bias in fishing mortality. The historical
2D AR1 sensitivity did not converge and retains its research status. The
50-jitter diagnostic recovered the best solution 48 times and found a poorer
mode twice; the age-3+ natural-mortality profile is shallow.

The scaled-back DSEM proof of concept compared two prespecified proxy edges
with the no-edge IID reference. The age-0 late-summer SST model had the lowest
AIC and reduced estimated residual recruitment variation by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * dsem_variance$variance_reduction_from_iid[dsem_variance$model == "late_summer_sst"])`%
relative to IID. The cold-pool edge received little support. This result
illustrates the Rceattle-DSEM connection, but the annual data do not yet
represent the prey, age-0 energy, overwinter-survival, and cannibalism
mediators required to attribute the association to a causal mechanism.

Immediate work should retain the ADMB-to-Rceattle comparison as a repeatable
numerical check, evaluate selectivity and survey influence on the retrospective
pattern, and continue sensitivity checks for the shared ATS/AVO annual
selectivity deviations. Given acceptance in other applications and the proven
bridging aspects, we feel this approach should be adopted for operational
management advice for November/December 2026. Future refinements will explore
trade-offs in fitting data in alternative ways (e.g., using random effects
approaches for selectivity variability, selecting alternatives to the
robust-multinomial approach used in this example). The exploratory DSEM work
provides a reproducible approach for adding cohort-aligned covariates, while
remaining separate from the final assessment configuration and projection
results.

## Appendices {.unnumbered}

### A-1 Reproducibility and analysis sequence {.unnumbered}

The working paper is rendered from saved model and diagnostic products so that
building the document does not repeat long model fits. The commands below are
run from the project directory, in the order shown when an earlier product is
required by a later analysis.

1. The [input-preparation script](<2024 EBS pollock setup data.R>) documents
   the transformations used to prepare the aligned Rceattle workbook; its
   precursor workbook is regenerated with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock setup data.R"`. The frozen workbook used for the
   reported fit is `Data/EBS_24_pollock_m23_rceattle_full_1964-2024.xlsx`.
   The same script documents the modified ADMB reference rebuild, run as
   `cd ADMB/m23_rceattle_full && admb pm && ./pm -nox -iprint 150` after the
   ADMB executable directory has been added to `PATH`.
2. The [two-stage fitting script](<2024 EBS pollock.R>) fits the reported
   Rceattle configuration and the 2D age-by-year AR1 sensitivity with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock.R"`. The
   [5.8.1 summary script](R/finalize_rceattle_5_8_1_analysis.R) then
   generates the fitted-model summaries and standard-multinomial sensitivity
   using `Rscript R/finalize_rceattle_5_8_1_analysis.R`.
3. The [ADMB bridge runner](R/run_canonical_pm_forward_bridge.R) sets the
   Rceattle parameters and realized selectivity to the ADMB values and saves
   the trajectory, likelihood, and gradient comparisons with
   `Rscript R/run_canonical_pm_forward_bridge.R`.
4. The [OSA runner](R/run_canonical_pm_diagnostics.R) generates the saved OSA
   residuals with `Rscript R/run_canonical_pm_diagnostics.R`. The
   [retrospective script](<2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R>) runs
   the nine terminal-year-consistent peels with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock two-stage retrospectives.R"`.
5. The [5.8.1 self-test runner](R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test.R) generates 50
   phased simulations with `Rscript R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test.R`. The
   [restart runner](R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test_restart.R) repeats the same
   simulations from the estimated solution with
   `Rscript R/run_rceattle_5_8_1_self_test_restart.R`, and the
   [validation summarizer](R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_validation.R) is run with
   `Rscript R/summarize_rceattle_5_8_1_validation.R`.
6. The [projection runner](R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R), which uses the
   [Rceattle-to-SPM input writer](R/write_spmr_projection_inputs.R), generates
   the seven-scenario and fixed-catch projection products with
   `Rscript R/run_spmr_tier3_projection.R`.
7. The [DSEM script](<2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R>) runs the four
   observed-covariate models with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R"` and the
   missingness-preserving randomized controls with
   `Rscript "2024 EBS pollock DSEM proof of concept.R" --randomized`.
8. After these saved products are available, the HTML and PDF are generated
   together with `quarto render ebswp.qmd`.
